_comment: Recommendation catalog for the distribution-list scan (Invoke-NRGAssessment.ps1 -DistributionListsOnly), read by Lib/Get-NRGDistributionListBaseline.ps1. ADVISORY and READ-ONLY: nothing here is scored in the assessment, and nothing here is ever executed. AdminCommands are TEXT printed in the worksheet for a human to review and run. Every recommended value is either Microsoft's documented default or guidance (Basis 'Microsoft') or an NRG judgment (Basis 'NRG'). An NRG judgment is never invented here: it names a StandardKey in Config/nrg-standards.json, which ships empty until the owner approves it, and an empty standard means 'not assessed', never 'met'. Every SourceUrl was opened on Microsoft Learn on 2026-10-02. Nist80053 is NRG's own mapping of each setting to the 800-53 Rev 5 control whose text it fits; it is not a quotation of NIST and not a statement that NIST addresses distribution lists. No CISA ScubaGear or CIS item written for distribution lists was found (ScubaGear 2.0.0 has none), so no such id is cited anywhere: the worksheet prints 'no framework item verified' instead of guessing.
NistMappingNote: NRG mapping of the setting to an 800-53 Rev 5 control, for the reader's own documentation. Not a quotation of NIST.

recommendations.Title: Distribution list accepts mail from outside senders
recommendations.Why: Microsoft documents that new distribution lists accept mail only from senders inside the organization by default, and that the other option ('Senders inside and outside of my organization') allows anyone, including people on the Internet, to send to the list. DMARC does not close this: it is evaluated for mail that claims your own domain in the From address, and it is not a recipient-side limit on who may send to a list. An all-staff list reachable from outside is reachable by whoever finds its address.

Distribution.Effect: The list accepts mail only from authenticated senders inside the organization; mail from outside the organization is rejected (Microsoft: True rejects unauthenticated, external senders).

Dynamic.Effect: The list accepts mail only from authenticated senders inside the organization; mail from outside the organization is rejected (Microsoft: True rejects unauthenticated, external senders).

recommendations.Title: Allowed senders limit who can send to the list
recommendations.Recommended: When the list must accept outside mail: an allowed-senders list limited to the people the list serves (for a list with external members, seeded from its current members)
recommendations.Why: Microsoft documents that AcceptMessagesOnlyFromSendersOrMembers specifies who is allowed to send to the list and that messages from other senders are rejected; individual senders (mailboxes, mail users, mail contacts) and groups are valid values, identified by name, alias, distinguished name, email address or GUID. To accept chosen outside senders, Microsoft's troubleshooting page (written for a mail user as the recipient; its delivery-restrictions page says other recipient types use the same parameters) says to represent each one with a mail contact or mail user, clear 'Require that all senders are authenticated' (RequireSenderAuthenticationEnabled False), and list the outside senders together with the internal senders or a group that holds them: everyone not on the list is rejected, internal staff included. The Exchange Online cmdlet reference states that RequireSenderAuthenticationEnabled True rejects unauthenticated (external) senders, so an external member cannot send to a list that requires authenticated senders. An allowed-senders list matches the sender's address; it does not authenticate an outside sender. The worksheet proposes a list built from the current members as a SNAPSHOT: a member added later is not on it.

Distribution.EmptyRestoreNote: Microsoft's cmdlet page names $null only as this parameter's default (blank) state and does not document clearing it with $null, and this has not been run against a tenant. The check after the rollback is what proves the state was restored: if it still lists entries, stop and clear the setting in the portal.
Distribution.Effect: Only the listed senders can send to the list. Mail from anyone else is rejected, staff who are not members included (Microsoft).

recommendations.Title: Hiding a list from the address list does not stop mail reaching it
recommendations.Recommended: Not an access control; do not rely on it
recommendations.Why: Microsoft documents that even when a list is hidden from the global address list, people can still send mail to it by typing the email address. A hidden list is not a protected list.

recommendations.Title: Distribution list has no owner
recommendations.Why: Microsoft states that each distribution list must have at least one owner. An ownerless list has no one accountable for who is in it, who may join, or who approves moderated mail.

Distribution.RollbackReason: The captured original state is no owner. Microsoft states every distribution list must have at least one owner, so this scan prints no command that writes 'no owner' back; treat adding an owner as one-way.
Distribution.Effect: The person you name becomes an owner of the list and can change its members and settings.

Dynamic.RollbackReason: The captured original state is no owner. Microsoft states every distribution list must have at least one owner, so this scan prints no command that writes 'no owner' back; treat adding an owner as one-way.
Dynamic.Effect: The person you name becomes an owner of the list and can change its settings.

recommendations.Title: Moderation is on but no one is named to approve mail
recommendations.Recommended: A named moderator, or an owner to receive approvals, whenever moderation is on
recommendations.Why: Moderation is off by default. Microsoft documents that when moderation is on and no moderator is selected, messages to the group are sent to the group owners for approval. A moderated list with no moderator and no owner has no one to approve its mail.

Distribution.EmptyRestoreNote: Microsoft's cmdlet page names $null only as this parameter's default (blank) state and does not document clearing it with $null, and this has not been run against a tenant. The check after the rollback is what proves the state was restored: if it still lists entries, stop and clear the setting in the portal.
Distribution.Effect: The person you name approves mail sent to the moderated list before it is delivered.

Dynamic.EmptyRestoreNote: Microsoft's cmdlet page names $null only as this parameter's default (blank) state and does not document clearing it with $null, and this has not been run against a tenant. The check after the rollback is what proves the state was restored: if it still lists entries, stop and clear the setting in the portal.
Dynamic.Effect: The person you name approves mail sent to the moderated list before it is delivered.

recommendations.Title: External members are shown, not judged
recommendations.Setting: Members (external mail contacts, mail users, guests)
recommendations.Recommended: No recommendation: external members are expected on a list that serves outside parties; what limits their exposure is who can send to the list (DL-1.1, DL-1.2)
recommendations.Why: Microsoft's page on managing distribution lists names mail contacts and mail users among the supported member types, which is how outside addresses become members, and makes no recommendation about outside members either way. This scan therefore reads and counts them (Class External in the member rows) and does not judge them, and it prints no command that removes one. What it does judge is who can send to the list, because a list that accepts mail from anyone and holds outside addresses sends everything mailed to it, internal replies and attachments included, to those addresses.

recommendations.Title: Distribution list has more members than the approved cap
recommendations.Recommended: At or under the approved NRG maximum
recommendations.Why: Microsoft's page on managing distribution lists makes no recommendation about maximum membership. A cap is an NRG judgment about how large a blast radius one address should have, so the finding is made only against an approved number. For a dynamic list the count is the calculated membership Microsoft stores on the group, refreshed about every 24 hours (or, when that cannot be read, a preview of its filter), so it can differ from who receives mail sent now.

recommendations.Title: Anyone can join the distribution list
recommendations.Recommended: Per the approved NRG standard for join restriction
recommendations.Why: Microsoft documents three join settings: Open (anyone can join without owner approval), Closed (only owners can add members) and ApprovalRequired (anyone may request, owners approve). Microsoft's Exchange Server 2013 page names Open as the default; the Exchange Online page lists the values without naming one, so this tool reads the actual value and recommends none of its own. Which setting NRG requires is an NRG judgment, so the finding is made only against an approved standard. An open list lets any user add themselves and receive everything sent to it.

Distribution.Effect: People can join the list only the way the new setting allows (Open: anyone; Closed: only owners add members; ApprovalRequired: owners approve requests).

recommendations.Title: A mail flow rule bypasses spam filtering (SCL -1) on a weak condition
recommendations.Recommended: No SCL -1 rule on a sender domain alone, on no sender condition, or on a domain you own; any bypass rule should carry a further condition such as Authentication-Results dmarc=pass or a restricted source IP
recommendations.Why: Microsoft: never configure a mail flow rule with only the sender domain as the condition to skip spam filtering, because that significantly increases the chance an attacker can spoof the domain, skip all spam filtering, and skip sender authentication checks. Microsoft also says not to use domains you own (accepted domains) or popular domains as conditions. A bypass rule applies to every recipient it matches, so it reaches every distribution list in scope of the rule. SCL -1 overrides spam filtering only: it cannot bypass malware or high confidence phishing filtering.

Inspect.Tenant: Get-TransportRule | Where-Object {$_.SetSCL -ne $null} | Format-Table Name, State, Priority, SetSCL

Tenant.Effect: Disables the WHOLE rule, not only its SCL -1 setting: every other action the rule takes stops too. Mail it matched is filtered like any other mail.

recommendations.Title: IP Allow List skips spam filtering for the listed addresses
recommendations.Recommended: Empty, or as few entries as possible, each /24 or smaller, none from consumer or shared infrastructure, reviewed regularly
recommendations.Why: Microsoft: keep the IP Allow List to a minimum, be as restrictive as possible, recommend an address range of /24 or less, do not use ranges that belong to consumer services or shared infrastructure, and review entries regularly. Mail from an allowed address skips spam filtering for every recipient, including every distribution list. Microsoft's own pages differ on whether such mail can still fail DMARC: the anti-spam troubleshooting page says the IP Allow List does not override DMARC failures, while the allowlist page says mail from allowed IPs skips SPF, DKIM and DMARC checks. The tool treats an allowed address as a spam-filtering bypass either way. Malware and high confidence phishing are still filtered.

Tenant.Effect: Mail from the removed addresses is no longer exempt from spam filtering, for every recipient.

recommendations.Title: Anti-spam policy lists allowed senders or allowed domains
recommendations.Recommended: None configured; if one is unavoidable, temporary and never a popular domain
recommendations.Why: Microsoft: avoid allowed sender and allowed domain lists in anti-spam policies if at all possible, because senders on them bypass spam, spoof and phishing protection (except high confidence phishing); the method is best used for temporary testing only, and attackers can spoof allowed domains. Never add common domains such as microsoft.com or office.com. By default these lists are not configured in the default anti-spam policy.

Tenant.Effect: Mail from the removed senders or domains is filtered like any other mail, for every recipient the policy applies to.

recommendations.Title: One of the tenant's own domains is on an allow list
recommendations.Setting: Transport rule SenderDomainIs and anti-spam allowed senders/domains, against Get-AcceptedDomain
recommendations.Recommended: No accepted domain on any allow list or bypass rule condition
recommendations.Why: Microsoft: do not use domains you own (accepted domains) as conditions in mail flow rules, because doing so creates opportunities for attackers to send email that would otherwise be filtered. For allowed sender and allowed domain lists in anti-spam policies, Microsoft notes that since September 2022 allowed senders, domains and subdomains in your own accepted domains must pass email authentication checks to skip spam filtering, so spoofed mail claiming your domain does not skip filtering by that route. An own-domain bypass rule carries no such note. Either way, an own-domain entry is a standing exception to the filtering your DMARC policy relies on.

recommendations.Title: Outlook Safe Senders (per mailbox) can bypass spam filtering
recommendations.Why: Microsoft documents that entries in a user's Safe Senders list make senders skip spam filtering for that mailbox, that this method creates a high risk of attackers delivering mail that would otherwise be filtered, and that it is not desirable in most situations. The list lives in each mailbox, so reading it means one query per mailbox; this scan does not do that, so the exposure is unmeasured, not absent.

recommendations.Title: Lookalike domains and display-name impersonation are not covered by DMARC reject
recommendations.Why: DMARC validates mail that claims your domain in the From address. A message from a different, real domain that looks like yours, or that uses an executive's display name from an unrelated address, is not a DMARC failure for your domain. Microsoft documents that impersonation can pass SPF, DKIM and DMARC when the attacker publishes valid DNS records for a lookalike domain, and that impersonation protection is part of Defender for Office 365 anti-phishing policies. This scan cannot detect either case, so a clean worksheet does not mean a list is safe from them.
